text: A GPS receiver in a phone or car can tell you where you are to within a few metres, but it never sends a signal to anything. Instead, it listens. Around thirty satellites orbit Earth for the Global Positioning System, and each one constantly broadcasts its position and the exact time. A receiver picks up signals from several satellites. Because radio signals travel at a known speed, the small difference between the time a signal was sent and the time it arrived reveals how far away that satellite is. With distances from several satellites, the receiver can work out the one place where it must be. The system was built for the United States military, but now the signals are free for anyone to use. GPS works best outdoors, because signals are weakened by thick walls and tunnels.

text: Leila had waited all week for a windy day, and now the flag at the end of the street was snapping like a whip. She carried the kite her grandfather had made up to the top of the hill. It was not as shiny as the plastic kites in the shops. Its frame was cane, its skin was bright red paper, and its tail was made of knotted ribbons. "It will never fly," muttered a boy nearby, but Leila pretended not to hear. She held the string tightly, ran down the slope, and let go. For a moment the kite wobbled and dipped towards the grass. Then a gust caught it, and it leapt upward as though it had been waiting for permission. Higher and higher it climbed, its ribbons dancing, until it was a small red spark in the sky. text: Jonas knew every line of the school play. He had practised in the shower, on the bus and even while brushing his teeth. But when the curtain opened and he saw two hundred faces in the dark hall, his mind went as blank as a clean whiteboard. His mouth was dry. Beside him, Priya, who played the queen, raised one eyebrow and waited. Jonas swallowed. Then, instead of the speech he had learned, he heard himself say, "Your Majesty, I have run so fast that I have forgotten my message!" A few people laughed, and Priya replied, "Then catch your breath, messenger, and tell me when you remember." Jonas took a slow breath, and the first line floated back into his head. The rest of the scene went smoothly. Afterwards, the teacher said that the best performers are not the ones who never slip, but the ones who keep going.

text: In a narrow lane lived a clockmaker named Mr Osei, who could mend any watch in the town. His apprentice, Lina, was quick with her hands but hated waiting. One morning, he handed her a tiny pocket watch that had stopped years before. "Do not hurry it," he said. Lina cleaned each gear and set each spring, but when she closed the case, the watch still did not tick. She sighed and wanted to give up. Instead, Mr Osei asked her to open it once more and look slowly. This time she noticed a speck of dust, almost too small to see, caught beneath a gear. She lifted it out with a fine pair of tweezers, and the watch began to tick. "The hardest faults to find," said Mr Osei, smiling, "are the ones we are too hurried to notice." Lina laughed, and for the first time she was not in a rush to start the next job.
